title: Protein synthesis
summary: How the base sequence of a gene is transcribed into mRNA and then translated by ribosomes and tRNA into a polypeptide, using the genetic code.

keyterms.definition: Synthesis of RNA using a DNA strand as a template, catalysed by RNA polymerase; the first stage of gene expression.
Enzyme that separates the DNA strands and links RNA nucleotides, paired to the template by complementary base pairing, into an RNA strand.
The DNA strand that is transcribed; the RNA is complementary to it and has the same base sequence as the coding strand, with U for T.
RNA transcribed from a gene that carries its base sequence, as a series of codons, to ribosomes for translation.
Synthesis of a polypeptide at a ribosome, with the amino acid sequence determined by the sequence of codons in mRNA.
Organelle of rRNA and protein, with small and large subunits, that binds mRNA and tRNA and catalyses peptide bond formation.
RNA molecule that carries a specific amino acid and has an anticodon that pairs with a complementary mRNA codon.
Sequence of three mRNA bases that codes for one amino acid or acts as a start or stop signal.
Sequence of three bases on a tRNA molecule that is complementary to, and pairs with, a codon on mRNA.
The 64 codons and their meanings; it is degenerate (several codons per amino acid) and almost universal across organisms.
Covalent bond formed by condensation between the amino group of one amino acid and the carboxyl group of another.
Disease caused by a base substitution in the β-globin gene (GAG→GTG) that replaces glutamic acid with valine in haemoglobin.
Non-coding DNA sequence near the start of a gene where RNA polymerase binds to initiate transcription.
Processing of eukaryotic pre-mRNA: introns are removed and exons spliced, and a 5' cap and 3' poly-A tail are added.
Joining different combinations of exons from the same pre-mRNA, so one gene can code for several polypeptide variants.
Protein complex that breaks down unwanted or damaged proteins into amino acids, which are recycled for new protein synthesis.

options: Synthesis of a polypeptide using the sequence of codons in mRNA
Production of an exact copy of a DNA molecule
Synthesis of RNA using a DNA strand as a template
Removal of introns from mRNA
questions.explanation: Transcription copies the base sequence of a gene into RNA. Making a polypeptide from mRNA is translation, and copying a whole DNA molecule is replication.

questions.statement: In transcription, an RNA nucleotide containing uracil pairs with adenine on the DNA template strand.
questions.explanation: RNA has uracil instead of thymine, so wherever the template has adenine, a uracil nucleotide is added by complementary base pairing (hydrogen bonding).

questions.text: The enzyme that separates the DNA strands and links RNA nucleotides during transcription is RNA ___.
questions.explanation: RNA polymerase both unwinds the DNA and joins RNA nucleotides; unlike replication, no separate helicase is needed.

questions.prompt: Put the events of transcription in order.
items: RNA polymerase binds to DNA at the start of a gene
RNA polymerase separates the two DNA strands by breaking hydrogen bonds
Free RNA nucleotides pair with complementary bases on the template strand
RNA polymerase links the nucleotides with covalent bonds
The RNA separates from the DNA and the double helix re-forms
questions.explanation: The bases must be exposed before nucleotides can pair with them; RNA polymerase then joins the paired nucleotides. Behind the polymerase the RNA peels away and the DNA strands rejoin.

questions.prompt: Match each base on the DNA template strand to the base added to the RNA.
questions.explanation: Pairing rules are the same as in DNA except that RNA uses uracil to pair with adenine. Thymine never appears in RNA.

questions.prompt: A DNA template strand has the sequence 3'-TACGGA-5'. What is the sequence of the mRNA transcribed from it?
options: 5'-ATGCCT-3'
5'-UACGGA-3'
5'-AUGCCU-3'
5'-TACGGA-3'
questions.explanation: Each template base is paired with its RNA complement (T→A, A→U, C→G, G→C), giving AUGCCU. ATGCCT is the coding-strand DNA sequence, which contains thymine, not uracil.

questions.statement: Transcription alters the base sequence of the DNA template, so a gene can only be transcribed a limited number of times.
questions.explanation: The template is only read, not changed: hydrogen bonds re-form and the original sequence is kept. This stability lets a gene be transcribed repeatedly throughout a cell's life.

questions.text: Only one of the two DNA strands of a gene, the ___ strand, is used to make the RNA.
questions.explanation: RNA is built complementary to the template strand, so its sequence matches the other, coding strand (with U in place of T). Leading and lagging strands are terms from DNA replication.

questions.prompt: A pancreatic β-cell and a skin cell from the same person contain the same genes, but only the β-cell makes insulin. What is the best explanation?
options: Skin cells have lost the insulin gene during development
Skin cells make insulin mRNA but their tRNA cannot translate it
The insulin gene is mutated in skin cells
The insulin gene is transcribed in β-cells but not in skin cells
questions.explanation: Not all genes are expressed in every cell. Transcription is the first stage of gene expression and a key control point: if a gene is not transcribed, its protein cannot be made.

questions.prompt: Why is it important that transcription does not change the DNA base sequence in a non-dividing cell such as a neuron?
options: Neurons do not need to make proteins after they have formed
The same genes must be transcribed accurately throughout the cell's life, which can last decades
Changed DNA would be passed to daughter cells by mitosis
RNA polymerase can only read DNA that has never been transcribed before
questions.explanation: A neuron cannot renew its DNA by replication and division, so its genes must stay unchanged to be transcribed for its whole life. DNA's stability as a template makes this possible.

options: Synthesis of a polypeptide using the sequence of codons in mRNA
Synthesis of mRNA using a DNA template
Folding of a polypeptide into its tertiary structure
Transport of mRNA from the nucleus to the cytoplasm
questions.explanation: At the ribosome, each mRNA codon is matched to a tRNA carrying a specific amino acid, so the codon sequence determines the amino acid sequence of the polypeptide.

questions.prompt: Match each component to its role in translation.

pairs.right: Carries the sequence of codons from the gene
Carries a specific amino acid and has an anticodon
Holds mRNA and tRNA and catalyses peptide bond formation
Three mRNA bases specifying one amino acid

questions.explanation: mRNA provides the coded message, tRNAs bring the matching amino acids, and the ribosome positions them and links them into a polypeptide.

questions.text: The sequence of three bases on tRNA that pairs with an mRNA codon is called an ___.
questions.explanation: The anticodon is complementary to the codon, so hydrogen bonding between them ensures the correct amino acid is added.

questions.statement: The genetic code is degenerate, meaning that more than one codon can code for the same amino acid.
questions.explanation: There are 64 codons but only 20 amino acids, so most amino acids have two or more codons (e.g. GAA and GAG both code for glutamic acid).

questions.statement: Each tRNA molecule can carry any amino acid, depending on which codon it binds to.
questions.explanation: Each type of tRNA, identified by its anticodon, has one specific amino acid attached to it. This fixed link between anticodon and amino acid is what makes translation reliable.

questions.prompt: Use the genetic code: AUG = Met, UGG = Trp, UUU = Phe, UAC = Tyr, ACC = Thr, AAA = Lys. Which tripeptide is coded for by the mRNA sequence AUG UGG UUU?
options: Tyr–Thr–Lys
Met–Trp–Phe
Phe–Trp–Met
Met–Thr–Phe
questions.explanation: The codon table is written for mRNA codons, so read AUG, UGG, UUU directly. Tyr–Thr–Lys comes from wrongly decoding the complementary anticodons (UAC, ACC, AAA).

questions.prompt: Put the steps of one cycle of polypeptide elongation in order.
items: A tRNA with an anticodon complementary to the next codon binds to the ribosome
A peptide bond links the growing polypeptide to the amino acid on this tRNA
The ribosome moves along the mRNA by one codon
The tRNA that has lost its amino acid is released
questions.explanation: Each cycle adds one amino acid: a matching tRNA arrives, the chain is joined to its amino acid by a peptide bond, the ribosome shifts one codon, and the empty tRNA leaves to be reloaded.

questions.text: Amino acids in the growing polypeptide are linked by ___ bonds.
questions.explanation: The ribosome catalyses a condensation reaction forming a peptide bond. Hydrogen bonds hold codon and anticodon together; glycosidic and phosphodiester bonds are found in carbohydrates and nucleic acids.

questions.prompt: What is meant by the genetic code being universal?
options: Every cell in an organism contains the same genes
Each amino acid is coded for by only one codon
All organisms make the same proteins
Almost all organisms use the same codons for the same amino acids
questions.explanation: With only minor exceptions, a codon means the same amino acid in bacteria, plants and animals. This is why a human gene can be expressed in bacteria to make, for example, human insulin.

questions.prompt: In sickle cell anaemia, one codon in the β-globin mRNA changes from GAG to GUG. What is the effect on the polypeptide?
options: Glutamic acid is replaced by valine at one position
Translation stops early, producing a short polypeptide
Every amino acid after the mutation is changed
No effect, because the genetic code is degenerate
questions.explanation: A single base substitution (A→T in DNA) changes one codon, so one amino acid changes from glutamic acid to valine. This makes haemoglobin form fibres at low oxygen, distorting red blood cells into a sickle shape.

questions.statement: RNA polymerase adds nucleotides to the 3' end of the growing RNA, so RNA is synthesised in the 5'→3' direction.
questions.explanation: Like DNA polymerase, RNA polymerase can only extend a strand at its 3' end, so transcripts grow 5'→3' while the template is read 3'→5'.

questions.prompt: Where does RNA polymerase bind to initiate transcription?
options: The start codon (AUG)
The promoter
The first intron
A telomere
questions.explanation: The promoter is a non-coding DNA sequence near the start of the gene; transcription factors binding there help RNA polymerase attach. AUG is a codon on mRNA used to start translation, not transcription.

questions.prompt: Put the events of the initiation of translation in order.
items: The small ribosomal subunit binds to the mRNA
An initiator tRNA carrying methionine pairs with the start codon AUG
The large ribosomal subunit binds, with the initiator tRNA in the P site
A second tRNA enters the A site and the first peptide bond forms
questions.explanation: Translation begins when mRNA binds the small subunit and the start codon is paired with the initiator tRNA (methionine). The large subunit then completes the ribosome, leaving the A site free for the next tRNA.

questions.prompt: Match each non-coding DNA sequence to its role.

pairs.right: Transcribed but removed from pre-mRNA before translation
Transcribed into functional RNA but never translated

questions.explanation: Much of the genome does not code for polypeptides: some sequences regulate gene expression, some are introns, some protect chromosome ends, and some are genes for tRNA and rRNA.

questions.text: The removal of introns and joining of exons in eukaryotic pre-mRNA is called ___.
questions.explanation: Splicing cuts out introns and joins the exons to make mature mRNA. Capping is the addition of the 5' cap, a separate modification.

questions.prompt: How can one eukaryotic gene code for more than one version of a polypeptide?
options: Different combinations of introns are translated in different cells
The ribosome reads the mRNA in different reading frames
Different combinations of exons are kept in the mature mRNA
The gene mutates differently in each cell type
questions.explanation: In alternative splicing, some exons may be included or skipped, so one pre-mRNA can yield several mature mRNAs and protein variants. Introns are always removed and are not translated.

questions.statement: In eukaryotes, a 5' cap and a 3' poly-A tail are added to mRNA, which help protect it from breakdown and assist translation.
questions.explanation: Both modifications occur after transcription in eukaryotes; they stabilise the mRNA, help it leave the nucleus and help ribosomes bind for translation.

questions.prompt: Pre-proinsulin is converted to insulin in two stages. Which description is correct?
options: Introns are removed from pre-proinsulin, then a poly-A tail is added
The signal peptide is removed to give proinsulin, then the C-peptide is removed, leaving A and B chains joined by disulfide bonds
Two molecules of proinsulin bond together to form insulin
Methionine is added to each end of the polypeptide
questions.explanation: Many polypeptides must be modified to become functional. The signal peptide is cut off in the rough ER, then the C-peptide is removed, leaving two chains held by disulfide bonds. Introns and poly-A tails belong to mRNA, not polypeptides.

questions.text: Unwanted or damaged proteins in the cytoplasm are broken down into amino acids by protein complexes called ___.
questions.explanation: Proteasomes break proteins down so their amino acids can be reused. Keeping a functional proteome needs this constant breakdown alongside protein synthesis by ribosomes.

questions.statement: Because ribosomes move along mRNA in the 5'→3' direction, the start codon lies nearer the 3' end of the mRNA than the stop codon.
questions.explanation: Translation starts near the 5' end at AUG and proceeds 5'→3' towards the stop codon, so the start codon is nearer the 5' end.
